Orchot Tzadikim 10:19: And if there is trouble, such as famine or pestilence or other calamities and the like, one should always worry lest his own sins caused the matter. For Achan trespassed on the sacred ban and several thousand fell (Joshua 7). And he should return to the Blessed Lord as best he can.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:20: Have we not found that Elijah did not speak with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi because a lion devoured a Jew within three parasangs near his town, for he should have prayed for mercy that no calamity occur in his vicinity (Makkot 11a) — therefore let one always fear such matters.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:21: And so we find, when there was a three-year famine in the days of David, he investigated by what sin the famine had come, and in the end found that it had come because of him (Yevamot 78b). Therefore, at every calamity, one should worry lest it came because of him.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:22: And if he has good fortune and ease, he should worry lest he be consuming, in this world, [the reward of] the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:23: If he is poor and afflicted with suffering, he should worry lest the poverty and suffering are the fruit of his own iniquities, with the principal still preserved for him in the World to Come. And if he became idle from Torah study because of the poverty and suffering, he should worry all the more.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:24: If he is learned in Torah, he should worry lest his deeds not match his learning. And if he is not learned, he should worry about this, for he cannot delve deeply into the root of piety. And if people honor him, he should be careful not to rejoice in that honor, but should worry lest he receive his reward through that very honor. And if he is learned but held in contempt in the eyes of the world, he should rejoice in this; yet he should worry that, since he is held in contempt, the world does not accept his rebukes.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:25: There are further benefits of worries and sighs, as found in Tana d'Vei Eliyahu (chapter 4): every sage of Israel who has genuine words of Torah, and sighs over the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He, and over the honor of Israel that has been diminished, and longs and looks forward to the honor of Jerusalem, and to the Temple, and to the salvation soon to flourish, and to the ingathering of the exiles — the Blessed Lord causes the Holy Spirit to rest within him.
Orchot Tzadikim 10:26: Therefore let him worry and weep over the Torah that has been forgotten, and sigh over those who fear the Blessed Lord who have been held in contempt, and be embittered over the diminishing of piety, and over Israel, the people of the Lord, who are trampled underfoot; and let him place Jerusalem at the height of his joy, and merit to see her rejoicing, as it is written (Isaiah 66:10), "rejoice with her in gladness, all you who mourn for her."
Orchot Tzadikim 10:27: May the Blessed Lord, in the abundance of His mercies, grant us merit to be among those who see the glory of Zion, as it is written (ibid. 52:8), "for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord returns to Zion"; and it says (ibid. 40:5), "and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken."
Orchot Tzadikim 11:2: Regret. This is when a person does a thing, and then turns back from it and is sorry for the deed. And it is a very upright path with respect to teshuvah, for whoever has sinned and regrets it is as though he had not sinned.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:3: And it is impossible to do teshuvah without regret, for his sins will never be atoned for if he does not regret them. Prayer, too, is not accepted without regret, for how can one say, "forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned," when he does not regret his sins?
Orchot Tzadikim 11:4: A parable: this is like a king whose servant offended him, and he seeks pardon from the king. If the servant does not regret it in his heart, and returns to commit the same offense every day, the king will be all the more angry with him. And likewise, whoever robs people, and comes every day to ask the king to forgive him, and returns again to rob — there is no doubt that this robber increases the king's wrath through his very request for forgiveness. Therefore let him regret, and pray, and confess, and resolve that he will not do so again — and then his prayer will be accepted.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:5: But whoever does a good deed and then regrets it — this is a bad trait. Therefore you must be careful never to regret your good deeds, lest you lose your reward. If you gave charity to a poor man, and after a while he angered you, be careful not to regret the good you did for him; for since your intent at the time of giving was for the sake of Heaven, behold, your reward is preserved for you.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:6: This trait is very disgraceful in the eyes of the world, when a person is not steadfast in his own affairs: when he says something today and regrets it tomorrow, and does not stand by his word; when he vows to fast, or to give charity, or to study Torah, and then regrets it — this is bad.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:7: And even though it is a good thing to regret an evil deed, it is good for a person to establish himself so that he need not keep changing from one practice to another and from one trait to another. And this is the ultimate good: that he reflect within himself, and clarify the good practices and traits, and conduct his soul by them, and consider, regarding everything he does, whether he can stand by it — and only then take hold of it. And let him not leap from one practice to another, for it is a very disgraceful trait to be inconsistent. And such a person is despised in the eyes of the world, even if he leaps from one good trait to another good trait, for there is no substance in his affairs and he cannot be relied upon.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:8: O son of man! Return while your regret is still of use, and do not delay until you come to the grave, for then you will regret, and there will be no remedy for that regret.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:9: If you did something against your fellow, regret it and go appease him. And if your fellow wronged you and regrets it, accept him. Even if you are uncertain whether he regrets it in his heart, so long as he clears himself before you, accept him. If you rebuked him with harsh words until he came to hate you, in the manner David said (Psalms 139:21), "and I strive with those who rise up against You" — do not regret that dispute; for if you were to regret it and ask his forgiveness, he would only be strengthened in his error.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:10: Regret is a path to all good deeds: if one goes about idle from the words of Torah, let him regret the idleness, and set his heart to occupy himself with Torah with all his ability. If he did not strengthen himself to pray with great intent, let him regret it and think: what have I done? At a time when I could have acquired the life of the World to Come, I occupied myself with vanities! And if he reaches advanced age, let him greatly regret that his days passed without service of the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 11:11: Take this great principle to heart: reflect in your heart on everything you have done, and on every commandment you were not careful about. Regret each one individually, and reflect and argue within your heart: how did I fail to pursue doing the will of my Creator, blessed be He? How did I abandon the good words and ethical teachings of the Sages? It follows that regret is a great remedy for all the commandments.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:2: Anger is a bad trait. And just as scab is a disease of the body, so anger is a disease of the soul. And our Sages said (Nedarim 22a): whoever is angry is dominated by every kind of Gehinnom, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 11:10), "and remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh." And "evil" refers only to Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 16:4), "the Lord has made everything for His own purpose, and even the wicked for the day of evil." And not only that, but he is also dominated by hemorrhoids, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:65), "and the Lord shall give you there a trembling heart, and failing of eyes, and sorrow of soul" — what is a thing that causes failing of the eyes and grieves the soul? You must say: this is hemorrhoids.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:3: And our Sages further said (ibid.): whoever is angry — even the Divine Presence is not important in his eyes, as it is said (Psalms 10:4), "the wicked, in the pride of his anger [does not seek Him]; God is not in any of his thoughts." He also forgets his learning and adds to his own foolishness, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools"; and it is written (Psalms 92:7), "nor does a fool understand this"; and it is written (Proverbs 13:16), "but a fool exposes his folly." And it is known that his sins are more numerous than his merits, as it is said (ibid. 29:22), "and a man given to wrath abounds in transgression." And his punishment is very great, as it is said (ibid. 19:19), "a man of great wrath shall bear the penalty."
Orchot Tzadikim 12:4: And you see that people, when they are angry and hold onto their anger, do not pay attention to what they are doing, and do many things in their anger that they would not do without anger. For anger drives a person's intellect from within him, until he multiplies angry words and enters into strife and provocations. Therefore it is impossible for an angry person to be saved from great sins. And so Elijah said to Rav Yehuda: do not become angry and you will not sin (Berachot 29b). And they said (Eruvin 65b): a person is recognized by three things, one of them being his anger. For at a time of anger a person is recognized: if his anger overpowers his wisdom, and he does things at a time of anger without the guidance of wisdom — by this his anger is recognized. If his wisdom overpowers his anger, and he does not speak or act out of anger in a way he would not act without anger — by this his wisdom is recognized. And the wise man said: there are three whom the Holy One, blessed be He, loves, and one of them is whoever does not become angry (Pesachim 113b). And our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 2:5): the impatient one cannot teach; for out of the greatness of his anger, his students are afraid to ask him their questions, lest he become angry with them. And even if they do ask, he has no patience to explain to his students all that is needed. He will also answer them in an angry manner, and because of this they will not understand. And the students, even though their teacher is angry with them, should ask and inquire carefully, and not worry about his anger, nor quarrel with their teacher. And of them our Sages expounded (Berachot 63b): "and pressing the nose brings forth blood" (Proverbs 30:33) — whoever is subjected to his teacher's anger once or twice and remains silent merits to understand monetary law and capital law. And the master said: there is nothing harder than monetary law and capital law.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:5: The angry man finds no favor in the eyes of his fellow creatures, and is hated by them, and because of this his deeds are not accepted in their eyes. And even if he has Torah and good deeds in hand, people do not learn from him.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:6: The angry man is a burden upon the members of his household, who constantly hear his anger and his complaints. And it is likely that he will come to harm because he casts excessive dread, as in the incident of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, whose household members sought to feed him a limb from a living animal [in their fear of him] (Gittin 7a).
Orchot Tzadikim 12:7: The angry man does not overlook the wrongs done to him and does not forgive, but constantly takes vengeance and bears a grudge. Anger brings a person to strife; when he is angry with his fellows, they will quarrel with him and he with them. And where there is strife, there is envy and hatred. And you already know the evils of strife, as will be explained in the Gate of Strife.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:8: Anger prevents a person's heart from all good things, for when a person is angry, he has no heart to show compassion for the poor. And of the Blessed Lord it is said (Habakkuk 3:2), "in wrath remember mercy" — and this is very far from the ways of flesh and blood.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:9: Anger nullifies a person's intent of heart in prayer, and the Divine Presence does not rest through anger.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:10: No angry man will become a great scholar, for anger drives his wisdom out of his heart, so that he cannot answer properly, nor rebuke properly, and all his words lack good sense. The angry man is deprived of ethical guidance and rebuke, for no one is permitted to reveal to him his errors and his disgraceful ways, since everyone is afraid to tell him about his affairs, because he will grow angry at them. And even if someone does rebuke him, he will not accept it from him because of his anger. The general rule of the matter: the angry man will not accept any good trait unless he removes anger from his heart. Just as the angry man does not accept rebuke from others, so he cannot rebuke others properly, for the Torah said (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him" — at first rebuke him gently and privately, and speak to him in soft, pleading words, that you say this for his own good, and then you will not bear sin because of him. But if you rebuke your fellow at first with a loud, raging voice and shame him, then you will bear sin because of him. And that friend will not accept rebuke from you, for such is the way of people: when a person comes at his fellow forcefully, his fellow hardens himself against him and will not submit to him. Of this the wise man said (Ecclesiastes 9:17), "the words of the wise, spoken gently, are heeded."
Orchot Tzadikim 12:11: And you already know of Hillel and Shammai, of whom those three converts said: the impatience of Shammai sought to drive us from the world; the humility of Hillel drew us near beneath the wings of the Divine Presence (Shabbat 31a). Because of the great humility that was in Hillel, no person could make him angry; for whoever restrains himself from anger acquires the trait of humility and compassion, for the trait of cruelty comes from burning wrath, as it is written (Exodus 22:23), "and My wrath shall grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword." And so, always alongside the burning of wrath, vengeance is written, as it is written (Deuteronomy 11:17), "and the Lord's wrath be kindled against you, and He shut up the heavens so that there be no rain, and the ground yield not its produce."
Orchot Tzadikim 12:12: Anger brings insolence upon a person, and because of anger he will not submit, and will also not admit the truth. And the wise man said: when you wish to form an association with a person, provoke him to anger. If he admits the truth to you at the time of his anger, associate with him; and if not, leave him.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:13: Anger leads to error. Who is greater to us than Moses our teacher, peace upon him, who became angry on three occasions and fell into error? As it is said (Leviticus 10:16), "and he was angry with Eleazar and Itamar"; and it is written (ibid. verse 17), "why have you not eaten the sin-offering in the holy place?" And it is said (Numbers 20:10), "hear now, you rebels"; and it is written (ibid. verse 11), "and he struck the rock." And it is written, "and Moses was angry with the officers of the army" (ibid. 31:14); and it is written (ibid. verse 21), "and Eleazar the priest said to the men of the army who went to battle, this is the statute of the law" — teaching that the halachah had been forgotten from Moses (Vayikra Rabbah 13:1). Now understand: if this happened to Moses our teacher, peace upon him, what will happen to the foolish who become angry? Therefore Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "do not hasten in your spirit to be angry."
Orchot Tzadikim 12:14: And be very careful not to do any damage out of your anger, for our Sages said (Shabbat 105b): whoever tears his garments, or scatters his money, or breaks vessels in his rage, should be in your eyes as though he worshipped idols. For this is the craft of the evil inclination: today it tells him, "do this," and tomorrow it tells him, "do that," until finally it tells him, "worship idols," and he goes and does it. And therefore it is written (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no strange god within you" — and what is this "strange god" that is within a person? You must say: this is the evil inclination. See how the evil inclination grows powerful at a time of anger.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:15: And Rabbi said there are four types among those with temperaments (Avot 5:11): easy to anger and easy to appease — his loss cancels his gain. Hard to anger and hard to appease — his gain cancels his loss. Hard to anger and easy to appease — a pious man. Easy to anger and hard to appease — a wicked man.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:16: And these four traits are said with regard to the righteous man, when he is angry at the good, or in worldly matters. But "hard to anger" toward those who commit transgressions and "easy to appease" toward them — this is a bad trait, being appeased toward the wicked. And how much more so one who is "easy to anger" toward the righteous and "hard to anger" toward the wicked, and "easy to appease" toward the wicked and "hard to appease" toward the righteous — this is a complete villain.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:17: Even though anger is a very bad trait, nonetheless a person must at times conduct himself with the trait of anger — such as to discipline the wicked, to cast dread upon the members of his household, and to instill his awe in his students. And when angry at the wicked, he should weigh his anger carefully. For because Moses our teacher, peace upon him, said of Reuben and Gad, "a breed of sinful men" (Numbers 32:14), his own great-grandson later became a priest for idols — even though he had been angry for the sake of Heaven. Everything requires proper measure, in all of a person's ways. And he should see how he performs the commandments, whether in his anger or in his laughter.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:18: A person who has the trait of anger within him, but forces himself to conduct his manner as though he were not an angry person, of him it is said (Proverbs 16:32), "better is one slow to anger than the mighty, and one who rules his spirit than one who takes a city." And "slow to anger" is one of the thirteen attributes said of the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:19: The wise man said: whoever's anger comes with forethought — composure and dignity will be seen upon him. But whoever's anger comes upon him without forethought — folly will be seen upon him.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:20: The wise man further said: whoever's anger and rage are fierce is not far from the insane. And whoever is accustomed to anger — his life is not truly life, and he is never joyful. And since he is never joyful, he does not accept what befalls him with love and joy, nor does he justify the [divine] judgment upon himself, nor can he serve the Blessed Lord with joy.
